section.title: The Triumphal Entry and the Temple
section.sectionRationale: The King arrives at His city. Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt to shouts of Hosanna, then acts as Lord of the temple, cursing a fruitless fig tree and cleansing the temple courts, two signs of judgment on a fruitless religious system. The withered tree the next morning interprets the cleansing, and when the leaders challenge His authority, Jesus silences them with a question about John. The final confrontation in Jerusalem has begun.
section.thesis: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the promised King and comes to His temple as its Lord, and finding it fruitless like the leafy fig tree, He enacts God's judgment on empty religion, calling instead for a house of prayer, faith, and forgiveness, while His authority, questioned by the leaders, is shown to be from heaven.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the triumphal entry; the cursing of the fig tree and the cleansing of the temple; the withered fig tree with teaching on faith and prayer; and the challenge to Jesus' authority.

units.label: The triumphal entry
units.note: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord

verses.text: As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two of His disciples
and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here.
If anyone asks, ‘Why are you doing this?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it and will return it shortly.’”
So they went and found the colt outside in the street, tied at a doorway. They untied it,
and some who were standing there asked, “Why are you untying the colt?”
The disciples answered as Jesus had instructed them, and the people gave them permission.
Then they led the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and He sat on it.
Many in the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others spread branches they had cut from the fields.
The ones who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: “{{hosanna|Hosanna}}!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”
“Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” “Hosanna in the highest!”
Then Jesus entered Jerusalem and went into the temple courts. He looked around at everything, but since it was already late, He went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

units.label: The fig tree and the temple
units.note: a house of prayer for all the nations

verses.text: The next day, when they had left Bethany, Jesus was hungry.
Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if there was any fruit on it. But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves, since it was not the season for figs.
Then He said to the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” And His disciples heard this statement.

When they arrived in Jerusalem, Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.
And He would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts.
Then Jesus began to teach them, and He declared, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of {{proseuche|prayer}} for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”
When the chief priests and scribes heard this, they looked for a way to kill Him. For they were afraid of Him, because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching.
And when evening came, Jesus and His disciples went out of the city.

units.label: The withered fig tree and faith

verses.text: As they were walking back in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from its roots.
Peter remembered it and said, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.”
“Have {{pistis|faith}} in God,” Jesus said to them.
“Truly I tell you that if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen, it will be done for him.
Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
And when you stand to pray, if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.”

units.label: The challenge to Jesus' authority
units.note: by what authority are You doing these things

verses.text: After their return to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking in the temple courts, and the chief priests, scribes, and elders came up to Him.
“By what {{exousia|authority}} are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You the authority to do them?”
“I will ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
John’s baptism, was it from heaven or from men? Answer Me!”
They deliberated among themselves what they should answer: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From men’...” they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet.
So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

hosanna.gloss: Hosanna, from the Hebrew hoshia-na, save now or save, we pray, a cry from Psalm 118 that had become a shout of praise. The crowds hail Jesus with the pilgrim psalm, welcoming Him as the one who comes in the name of the Lord and the bearer of David's kingdom.

proseuche.gloss: Prayer. Quoting Isaiah, Jesus declares that the temple was meant to be a house of prayer for all the nations, a place of access to God for the whole world. The traders had made the court of the Gentiles a marketplace, robbing the nations of that access.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust in God. In light of the withered tree and the coming end of the temple system, Jesus calls His disciples to have faith in God, a confident, forgiving, prayerful trust that lays hold of God's power for what accords with His will.

exousia.gloss: Authority, the right to act. The leaders demand to know by what authority Jesus cleanses the temple and teaches. His authority is heavenly, of a piece with John's, and their refusal to answer honestly exposes their own lack of any authority to judge Him.

basic.context: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding a colt, and the crowds throw down cloaks and branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing the coming kingdom of David. He enters the temple, looks around, and leaves. The next day, hungry, He curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit. Then He enters the temple and drives out the traders, declaring that God's house was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations, not a den of robbers. The next morning the fig tree is withered to its roots, and Jesus teaches His disciples to have faith in God, to pray believing, and to forgive. When the leaders demand to know by what authority He acts, He asks whether John's baptism was from heaven; unable to answer without exposing themselves, they say they do not know, and Jesus refuses to answer them.
basic.hermeneutics: The fig tree and the temple cleansing interpret each other: Mark wraps the cleansing inside the fig tree story so we see the temple, like the tree, as all show and no fruit, under God's judgment. Jesus comes as King and as Lord of the temple. The teaching on faith, prayer, and forgiveness points beyond the doomed temple to a new access to God. The authority question shows the leaders' bad faith.
basic.originalLanguages: The crowds cry hosanna, save now, from Psalm 118. Jesus says the temple should be a house of proseuche, prayer, for all nations. He calls for pistis, faith, in God. And the leaders demand by what exousia, authority, He acts.
basic.typology: The King on the colt fulfils Zechariah's prophecy of the humble King coming to Zion. The fruitless fig tree is a prophetic sign-act of judgment on Israel's leadership. The cleansed temple and its coming end point to Jesus Himself as the true temple and to the access to God He opens for all nations.
basic.christ: Jesus is the King who comes in the name of the Lord, the Lord who comes to His temple in judgment, and the one whose authority is from heaven. He is the true meeting place between God and people.
basic.god: God comes to inspect His house and finds it fruitless. God desires His house to be a place of prayer for all peoples, and He judges the religion that has become a racket. God calls His people to faith, prayer, and forgiveness.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 9 foretells the humble King on a colt. Isaiah 56 and Jeremiah 7 lie behind the temple saying. Psalm 118 supplies the Hosanna.
basic.oneStory: The King long promised rides into His city, and the Lord comes to His temple, but He finds it fruitless and enacts its judgment, as He did the fig tree. The old house of stone, meant to be a house of prayer for all nations, has failed; Jesus Himself will become the true temple through His death and resurrection, opening access to God for the whole world.

context.literary:
Mark 11 opens the Jerusalem section, which occupies the rest of the Gospel, and Mark organises it by days. Jesus arrives on the first day, looks around the temple and leaves, 11:11. On the second day He curses the tree and clears the courts, 11:12 to 19. On the third morning the tree is seen withered and Jesus is challenged in the temple, 11:20 to 33. The temple discourse that follows in chapters 12 and 13 grows out of this day.

The fig tree frames the cleansing in Mark's familiar sandwich. The cursing, verses 12 to 14, opens the story; the cleansing, verses 15 to 19, forms the middle; and the withered tree, verses 20 to 25, finishes it. Each half explains the other. The tree with leaves but no fruit becomes a picture of a temple full of activity but without the fruit God sought, and the temple's fate is announced by the tree's.

The chapter is held together by the verb 'to see.' Jesus 'looked around at everything,' 11:11, and then 'saw' a tree in leaf, 11:13. The disciples later 'saw' it withered, 11:20. The opening scene has a deliberate pause: a King arrives, and nothing happens, because He has come to inspect first. Mark lets the entry end in anticlimax, an empty temple at evening, to show that the acclaim of the crowd is not the whole story.

The last scene is a trap that fails. The leaders ask by whose authority Jesus acts, and He answers with a question about John. Verse 26 does not appear in the earliest manuscripts, so the chapter's final saying on prayer is verse 25, and the controversy moves on to chapter 12.
context.historical:
Jesus approached Jerusalem from the east, down the Mount of Olives, past Bethphage and Bethany. The Mount of Olives carried hopes about the coming of the LORD, Zechariah 14:4, and a prophet coming from that side would have recalled such promises. In 1 Kings 1:33 to 40 Solomon rode a royal mule to be anointed, and in 2 Kings 9:13 the people spread their garments under Jehu on the steps and proclaimed him king. Spreading cloaks on the road was a royal gesture.

The animal on which no one had sat resonates with the sacred use of animals that had never been put under a yoke, Numbers 19:2. The disciples' answer, 'The Lord needs it,' is a request that a king might make, though Mark does not tell us more about the owner.

The temple Herod rebuilt was a vast complex. The outer court was open to Gentiles, who could come no further, and it was in this space that animals for sacrifice were sold and Temple coinage was exchanged, because pilgrims coming from afar needed approved animals and the annual tax was paid in a particular coin. Money changers and dove sellers were a convenience, and the poor who could afford only doves depended on them. Jesus' complaint is not that commerce was needed but that it had taken over the one space set aside for the nations. The carrying of goods as a shortcut through the courts, verse 16, treated the sacred ground as a road.

The fig tree is the other piece of local colour. Fig trees put out leaves in spring, and the small early figs that appear with the leaves were a sign that a crop would follow. A tree in leaf in the weeks before Passover promised something and delivered nothing. The leaders who confront Jesus are the three groups of the Sanhedrin, the chief priests, scribes and elders, so this is a formal challenge by the nation's governing body.
context.canonical:
The entry draws on Zechariah 9:9, a King who comes humble and riding on a colt, and on Psalm 118:25 to 26, one of the psalms sung at the pilgrim feasts, which Mark places in the crowd's mouth. Genesis 49:10 to 11 speaks of the ruler from Judah and his colt, and Malachi 3:1 promises that the Lord would suddenly come to His temple, a verse that Mark's opening quotation, 1:2, has already set in motion.

The temple saying combines two prophets. Isaiah 56:6 to 8 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will be brought to His mountain and that His house will be a house of prayer for all the nations, and Solomon himself had prayed that foreigners who prayed toward the temple would be heard, 1 Kings 8:41 to 43. Jeremiah 7:9 to 11 is the setting of the den of robbers. In that sermon the people thought the temple made them safe, and the prophet warned that the house would be destroyed. The fig tree echoes Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10 and Micah 7:1, where a tree without fruit is a picture of Israel.

The New Testament draws the threads together. Jesus is accused of threatening the temple, Mark 14:58, and John explains that He spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19 to 21. The veil tears, 15:38, and the church is described as a temple built on Christ the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19 to 22 and 1 Peter 2:4 to 5. In the end John sees no temple in the city, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark's readers lived in the shadow of the temple's destruction, or soon would, and they had to understand why the centre of Israel's worship fell. Mark tells them it was not an accident of politics. The King came, was welcomed with shouts, and found a house without fruit. The act of judgment, enacted first on a tree, was His.

Mark also wants his readers to see that the end of the old temple is not the end of access to God. Immediately after the cleansing he gives Jesus' teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness, which is the practice of the new house. The disciples, who will no longer have the temple as the place of meeting with God, are told to have faith in God, to pray, and to forgive. The quotation 'for all the nations' is retained in Mark alone among the Synoptics, which fits a Gospel written for a mixed community.

The passage also presents a question of authority. The leaders' demand shows they will not accept the answer and are willing to lie rather than commit themselves. Mark wants his readers to see that unbelief is often not lack of evidence but a decision to protect position.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The entry, the cursing of the tree and the cleansing of the temple are unique events in Jesus' ministry. Believers are not told to curse trees or to overturn tables, and nothing here authorises violence to enforce religious standards. Jesus acts with a right that belongs to Him as Lord of the temple.

What is prescriptive is what He says about prayer, faith and forgiveness in verses 22 to 25, and what He shows about worship. The church is to be a house of prayer open to the nations, and Christians are to ask whether the activity of any church has crowded out prayer and welcome. The temptation to tolerate a religion of busy appearances is a standing one, and the warning of the fig tree applies. The promise about mountains must be read with the rest of the New Testament: 1 John 5:14 ties confident prayer to what accords with God's will, and Jesus Himself prays 'not what I will,' Mark 14:36. The word about forgiveness is a direct command.

debates.question: Why did Jesus curse a fig tree for having no fruit when it was not the season for figs?

views.label: A prophetic sign-act against fruitless Israel
views.case: The leafy but fruitless tree pictures the temple and its leaders, all outward show and no fruit; Jesus curses it as an enacted parable of the judgment about to fall, not out of mere frustration.

views.label: A lesson in genuine versus pretended fruitfulness
views.case: A fig tree in full leaf normally bears early fruit; its bare branches were a false advertisement, symbolizing a religion that promises much and yields nothing, which God will not tolerate.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the tree is a living parable: God comes seeking fruit, and finding only leaves, He judges the pretense, a warning framed around the temple cleansing it encloses.

debates.question: What is the meaning of Jesus' promise about moving mountains by faith?

views.label: Confidence in God's power for His purposes
views.case: In context, this mountain may point to the temple mount whose end Jesus foretells; faith lays hold of God to accomplish what seems impossible when it accords with His will, as the withering tree has just shown.

views.label: A call to believing, forgiving prayer
views.case: Jesus binds the promise to prayer and forgiveness, verses 24 and 25; the emphasis falls on wholehearted trust in God and a heart cleared of grudges, not on treating faith as a technique to command God.

debates.bearing: Both hold that the point is confident trust in the living God, exercised in prayer and forgiveness, not a formula guaranteeing whatever we desire regardless of God's will.

debates.question: What was Jesus doing when He cleared the temple courts?

views.label: Cleansing a corrupted place
views.case: On this reading the trade in animals and currency had crowded out prayer and exploited worshippers, so Jesus restores the court to its purpose. His quotation of Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 accuses the leaders of turning a house of prayer into a hideout for those who feel safe while doing wrong.

views.label: An enacted sign of the temple's coming end
views.case: Mark's framing with the fig tree, and Jesus' later words, 13:1 to 2, suggest the act is not reform but a symbol of judgment. Jeremiah 7 was spoken in the days before the first temple fell, and Jesus borrows its words as the prophet did. The charge at His trial about destroying the temple, 14:58, shows how seriously the act was taken.

views.label: A claim of messianic authority over the temple
views.case: Jesus acts as one with the right to purge God's house, and the leaders' immediate question about authority in 11:28 shows they read it that way. Malachi 3:1 promises that the Lord would suddenly come to His temple, and the act can be read as that arrival.

debates.bearing: The views are compatible. A judgment on the temple's failure, a claim to authority over it and a restoration of its purpose for the nations are all present, and Mark sets them side by side so that the reader sees the Lord of the temple at work.

study.originalLanguages:
The crowd greets Jesus as 'He who comes in the name of the Lord,' ho erchomenos, 'the coming one.' The participle was becoming a title for the expected deliverer, and John the Baptist uses the same phrase when he asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come, Matthew 11:3. The disciples tell the owner 'the Lord needs it,' kyrios, a word that can mean owner, master or the divine Lord, and Mark leaves the double sense open.

When Jesus enters the temple Mark says He 'looked around at everything,' periblepo. The verb is a favourite of Mark's for the searching look of Jesus, as in 3:5 and 10:23, and it makes the visit an inspection. Mark uses hieron for the temple courts here, the whole complex, and mostly uses naos for the sanctuary itself, which is where the veil is torn in 15:38.

He 'drove out,' ekballo, the sellers, the verb used elsewhere in Mark for casting out demons, 1:34, and when the Spirit sent Jesus into the wilderness, 1:12. He 'overturned,' katastrepho, the tables of the money changers, kollybistai. The 'den of robbers,' spelaion leston, is the Septuagint phrase of Jeremiah 7:11, and lestes means a brigand, a violent person, not a petty thief, so the picture is of a hideout. Only Mark includes 'for all the nations,' pasin tois ethnesin, which Matthew and Luke leave out.

The tree is 'withered from its roots,' exerammene ek rhizon, so the damage began at the base. Jesus tells them, 'Have faith in God,' echete pistin theou. The genitive can mean faith directed to God, which is the usual reading, or God's own faithfulness. The saying about the mountain asks the one who prays not to 'doubt,' diakrino, a word meaning to be divided within, as James uses it of the double-minded, James 1:6. 'Believe that you have received it' translates a verb in the aorist, elabete, which some manuscripts replace with the present, and the sense is a confidence that rests on God's promise before the answer is seen. On forgiveness, 'forgive,' aphiemi, is the usual verb of release, and Jesus says to do it as you 'stand' praying, the usual posture of prayer.

The leaders ask, 'by what authority,' and Jesus asks them whether John's baptism was 'from heaven,' a common way of saying 'from God.' They 'reasoned,' dialogizomai, among themselves, the verb used of the scribes in 2:6 to 8 who reasoned in their hearts that Jesus blasphemed. Now it is they who are caught in their own reasoning. Their answer, 'We do not know,' ouk oidamen, is the confession of the teachers of Israel that they cannot judge a prophet.

typology.type: The king entering on a colt, Zechariah 9:9 and 1 Kings 1
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah describes the King who comes to Zion 'righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt.' Solomon rode David's mule to be anointed, and Jehu was hailed with garments on the steps. Jesus is acclaimed in the same pattern, but He comes in peace and not on a warhorse. The correspondence is of arrival and acclamation; the escalation is that the King comes to be enthroned by dying, not by overthrowing Rome. The type falls short in that Solomon's reign ended and Jehu's was bloody, while Jesus' kingdom is the one Zechariah says will extend from sea to sea, Zechariah 9:10.

typology.type: The fruitless fig tree, Jeremiah 8:13 and Hosea 9:10
typology.fulfillment: In the prophets Israel is a fig tree or vine from which God expects fruit. Hosea says God found Israel like early fruit on a fig tree, and Jeremiah says there will be no figs on the tree. Jesus' act with the tree is an enacted version of these oracles. The correspondence is of leaf without fruit; the escalation is that the judgment falls at the temple, the centre of the nation's life. The type is not a declaration against the Jewish people as such, since Jesus' disciples and the first church were Jewish, but against a leadership and a system that offered show without fruit. The tree falls short as a picture because trees cannot repent, while people can.

typology.type: The temple as God's dwelling, 1 Kings 8 and Ezekiel 11:23
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's temple was the place where God's name dwelt, and where foreigners could pray, 1 Kings 8:41 to 43. When the people profaned it, Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the city, Ezekiel 11:23. Jesus comes as the Lord returning to His temple, Malachi 3:1, and finding it unready. The escalation is that He Himself is the true dwelling of God among people, John 2:19 to 21, and later the church is called a temple, Ephesians 2:21 to 22. The type falls short because a building of stone could be defiled and destroyed, while the new temple is raised in three days and cannot be taken.

typology.type: The house for all nations, Isaiah 56:7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah promised foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD that they would be brought to the holy mountain and that their offerings would be accepted. The court of the Gentiles was where that promise should have been visible. Jesus' act on their behalf is a sign that the promise is about to be fulfilled in a different way. The correspondence is of nations and prayer; the escalation is that in Christ the dividing wall is broken down, Ephesians 2:14 to 18. The type falls short because Isaiah's picture still has the nations coming to a place, while in the new covenant God's presence goes out to them.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first as King. He does what the Old Testament said the King would do, rides the colt, receives the psalm, and comes to the city. He accepts the acclamation of the crowd and does not silence it, though Mark has taken care elsewhere to show Jesus hushing such talk. The time of concealment is ending, and the public identification of Jesus as the coming One is part of how He brings the confrontation to a head.

It leads to Christ as Lord of the temple. In Malachi 3:1 the Lord comes to His temple and the people do not recognise Him. In Mark 11 He enters, looks at everything, and returns the next day to act. The leaders' question about authority is the right one, and the answer is that He acts as the Son who owns the house, a point Mark will make in the parable of chapter 12.

It leads to Christ as the replacement of the temple. When Jesus teaches in the temple courts, the leaders look for a way to destroy Him, 11:18, and it is the charge that He would destroy the temple that is brought at His trial, 14:58. John tells us what He meant: the temple of His body, John 2:21. At His death the veil is torn, Mark 15:38, and the way to God is open. The church is then built on Him, Ephesians 2:20 to 22.

It leads to Christ as the one whose authority is from heaven. His question about John is not an evasion; it is a claim. The baptism of John pointed to the one who was to come, Mark 1:7 to 8, and to reject John was to reject Jesus. The one who is 'beloved Son' in the parable of the vineyard, 12:6, is the one asking.

It also leads to Christ as the one on whom the curse falls. The fig tree withers because Jesus pronounced judgment, and a few days later He will bear the judgment Himself. The way the Gospel is built should make us slow to read the tree as a simple threat; it is also a promise that the one who judges is the one who suffers for those under it.

A caution: not every detail is an allegory. The colt, the cloaks and the branches are not codes; Mark and the Old Testament give the links.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the one who comes. The King arrives, the Lord enters His temple, and the long prayer of the Psalms, 'save us, we pray,' is about to be answered, though not in the way the crowd expects. God does not wait for people to find Him but comes in His Son to those who claim to serve Him.

It shows God inspecting His house. The first day ends with Jesus looking at everything and leaving, and the second day brings the act. This patience should not be mistaken for indifference. God sees the whole place before He speaks, and His judgment follows knowledge. The leaders cannot say He acted rashly.

It shows that God seeks fruit. The tree is not condemned because it lacks the fruit of the wrong season, but because its leaves promised what it did not give. God's concern is not with ritual precision but with a people who produce what matches what they claim. Isaiah and Jeremiah say the same, and this is the standard by which the temple is judged.

It shows God's heart for the nations. His house was to be a place of prayer for all peoples, and the crowding of the outer court was a direct offence to that purpose. The God of Israel is the God who wants all peoples to pray to Him. Any religion that blocks the way for outsiders sets itself against Him.

It shows God as the hearer of prayer and the God who forgives. Jesus says that whatever is asked in prayer in faith will be given, and ties it to forgiveness, so that the one who has been forgiven by the Father must forgive others. God's readiness to answer is matched by His insistence that the pray-er is reconciled.

For worship, the passage asks whether our own gatherings are houses of prayer or houses of display, and whether the prayers we offer rest on His promise and not on our performance.

crossReferences.note: The prophet calls the daughter of Zion to rejoice because her King comes righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey. The disciples' fetching of the colt makes the prophecy visible, though Mark leaves it unquoted and lets the action speak.

'Save us, we pray' and 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD' were sung by pilgrims at the feasts. The crowd's cry gives Jesus the words of that welcome, and the same psalm supplies the rejected stone that Jesus quotes in 12:10 to 11.

The Lord whom the people seek will suddenly come to His temple. Mark began by quoting the opening line of this verse, 1:2, and in chapter 11 the Lord comes to the temple and finds it unready, which is the sense of the sudden arrival the prophet describes.

God promises that foreigners who join themselves to Him will be brought to His holy mountain and that His house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations. Jesus quotes this to show what the court of the Gentiles was for, and why the trade in it was an offence.

Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and told people who thought the building made them safe that it had become a den of robbers. Jesus takes the phrase and applies it, which means the sin lies in confidence in the building while living in a way God hates.

God says there will be no figs on the tree and even the leaf will wither. Jesus' cursing of the tree is a living version of this oracle, and the withering of the leaf in Mark 11:20 recalls the prophet's picture of a people whose appearance of life is taken away.

God says He found Israel like the firstfruits of the fig tree, and then the people went to Baal-peor. The image of Israel as a tree that should have borne fruit helps explain why Jesus looks for figs and why the nation's leaders are the target.

Solomon prays that the foreigner who comes and prays toward this house will be heard, so that all peoples will know God's name. The prayer shows that the temple was intended from the start to serve the nations, and that the outer court's use as a market betrayed it.

John records Jesus' claim that He would raise the temple in three days, and explains that He meant the temple of His body. It supplies the explanation for the charge in Mark 14:58 and for how the old house gives way to the new.

Paul describes believers as built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone, forming a holy temple in the Lord. Where Mark 11 shows the old temple under judgment, Ephesians shows the people of God as the new dwelling place.

Jesus tells His disciples that faith the size of a mustard seed can say to a mountain, 'Move from here to there.' The saying shows that the language of Mark 11:23 is a vivid way to express what faith in God can do, and not a technique.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden that was the first sanctuary, where God walked with His people. After the fall the story is about how God can live among people again. The tabernacle, then the temple, were God's answers: a house where His name dwelt, where sacrifice was made, and where, as Solomon prayed, the nations might come and know Him. The prophets who watched the temple's decline, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, saw the glory leave, and Malachi ended the Old Testament with the promise that the Lord Himself would suddenly come.

In Mark 11 that promise arrives, and not in the way many expected. The Lord comes to His temple on the back of a colt, looks around, and finds a house with leaves and no fruit. His acts, the tree and the tables, are the prophets' warnings made visible. Yet the passage does not end with destruction. It ends with Jesus teaching a different kind of house: people who have faith in God, who pray, and who forgive. The temple that was meant for the nations will be rebuilt in a way that includes them.

The story moves quickly. Within days He will be arrested on a charge about the temple, the veil will be torn, and the way into God's presence will be opened by His death. After His resurrection the Spirit comes on the church, which Paul and Peter call a temple and a priesthood, built on Christ. The picture of Ephesians 2 is of Jew and Gentile together, which is what Isaiah 56 promised and the court of the Gentiles was meant to serve.

The end of the Bible completes the picture. John sees no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The gates are never shut and the nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:24 to 26. The fig tree's lesson is not the last word. The tree of life stands at the centre of the city and bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:2, so that what God sought in vain in Jerusalem He finds in His people at last.

quiz.q: What did the crowds' welcome of Jesus into Jerusalem signify?

options.text: They hailed Him as the King coming in the name of the Lord, welcoming the coming kingdom of David.
options.note: Mark 11:9-10; the Hosanna and Psalm 118 shouts are a royal, messianic welcome.

options.text: They welcomed a respected teacher passing through the city.
options.note: Their cries of Hosanna and kingdom of David hailed far more than a teacher; they welcomed the messianic King.

options.text: They celebrated a prophet entering for the Passover feast.
options.note: There is truth here, but the shouts specifically acclaim the coming Davidic kingdom, not merely a prophet.

options.text: They demanded He lead a revolt against Rome.
options.note: The crowds praised Him with a pilgrim psalm; Jesus came as a humble King, not a military rebel.

quiz.q: How do the fig tree and the temple cleansing relate?

options.text: The fruitless leafy tree is a sign of the fruitless temple, both under God's judgment for show without substance.
options.note: Mark wraps the cleansing inside the fig tree story so each interprets the other.

options.text: They are two unrelated events that happened close together.
options.note: Mark deliberately intertwines them so the tree interprets the temple's judgment.

options.text: Both show Jesus acting in judgment on empty religion.
options.note: True, but it should note the pointed link: the barren tree pictures the fruitless temple.

options.text: Both show Jesus was simply hungry and frustrated.
options.note: The cursing and cleansing are prophetic sign-acts of judgment, not mere frustration.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say God's house was meant to be?

options.text: A house of prayer for all the nations, which they had made a den of robbers.
options.note: Mark 11:17 joins Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11.

options.text: A place of sacrifice for the people of Israel.
options.note: Sacrifice had its place, but Jesus stressed prayer and access for all nations, which the market had displaced.

options.text: A place of worship where God is honoured.
options.note: True but general; Jesus specifically said a house of prayer for all the nations, now made a robbers' den.

options.text: A marketplace to serve the many pilgrims.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus drove out the market that had corrupted the house of prayer.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about faith and prayer after the fig tree withers?

options.text: To have faith in God, to pray believing, and to forgive others so the Father will forgive us.
options.note: Mark 11:22-25 binds faith, believing prayer, and forgiveness together.

options.text: That faith can accomplish anything we wish for, without condition.
options.note: The promise is set within trust in God's will and joined to forgiveness, not an unconditional blank cheque.

options.text: To trust God confidently in prayer and to forgive others.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should also name believing that you have received what accords with God's will.

options.text: That prayer is unnecessary if you have enough faith.
options.note: Jesus commands believing prayer; faith and prayer go together, not one instead of the other.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond when the leaders demanded to know His authority?

options.text: He asked whether John's baptism was from heaven or men, exposing their bad faith when they refused to answer.
options.note: Mark 11:29-33; their evasion revealed they would not submit to heaven's authority.

options.text: He plainly told them His authority came from God.
options.note: He did not answer directly; He exposed their unwillingness to acknowledge the truth about John and Himself.

options.text: He answered their question with a question that unmasked their hypocrisy.
options.note: Accurate, but it should name the specific question about John's baptism and their fear-driven evasion.

options.text: He refused to speak to them at all.
options.note: He did engage them, posing a searching question before declining to answer their challenge.

questions: The crowds shouted Hosanna, yet many would soon call for His crucifixion. Where might your praise of Jesus be shallow or conditional, and how can it become true allegiance?
Jesus found leaves but no fruit. If He came looking for fruit in your life today, what would He find beneath the outward show?
God's house was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations. How does that shape the way you think about prayer and about welcoming outsiders to God?
Jesus joined believing prayer with forgiving others. Is there someone you are holding something against that is hindering your prayers?
The leaders would not honestly face the question about John. Where are you tempted to dodge the truth about Jesus rather than submit to His authority?

translationNotes.note: Hosanna transliterates the Hebrew hoshia-na, save now or save, we pray, from Psalm 118:25-26; a plea for salvation that had become a shout of joyful praise at the pilgrim feasts.

The BSB does not print a verse 26, since the words some manuscripts add, about the Father not forgiving if we do not forgive, are drawn from Matthew 6:15 and absent from the earliest witnesses here; the numbering skips from 25 to 27.
From heaven means from God, the source of true authority behind both John and Jesus.
